tldr: The authors developed "MuJoCable," a reduced-order cable transmission plugin for MuJoCo that simultaneously resolves moving contact on noncircular surfaces, unilateral tension (pull-only), and segment friction losses, reproducing transmission phenomena that cause sim-to-real gaps in tendon-driven robots with high accuracy and faster-than-real-time speed.
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram of MuJoCable. (a) Even with identical cable retraction, the robot's deformation and transmitted force change significantly depending on routing surface geometry, friction, and tension states. (b) The proposed method resolves smooth surface contact and friction, removing the limitations of native MuJoCo tendons (spring laws that exert pushing forces and restriction to spherical/cylindrical wraps).
overview:
Tendon transmissions (cable transmissions) are widely used in dexterous robot hands, continuum robots, and rolling contact mechanisms to reduce distal inertia and add compliance. However, the physical behavior of transmission systems—such as contact points where cables wrap and slide over body surfaces, slack, and friction at guide eyelets—is extremely complex. Native tendons in mainstream rigid-body simulators like MuJoCo only support simple wrapping around spheres or cylinders. Furthermore, they are computed as bidirectional springs, which incorrectly causes cables to exert "pushing forces." On the other hand, beam models that resolve free-form geometry (such as Cosserat rods) introduce too many degrees of freedom, dramatically increasing computational load.

To solve this, the authors propose "MuJoCable," a reduced-order plugin that neglects free-cable bending vibrations while jointly resolving moving contact surfaces, a unilateral tension law, and tension propagation via Capstan friction. The cable path across adjacent surface meshes and cylinders is optimized at every time step, and nodal forces are transmitted to rigid-body dynamics using the principle of virtual work.

For validation, the authors first verified consistency against analytical solutions across seven pulley benchmarks, demonstrating that theoretical transmission ratios and torques are accurately reproduced. Next, simulations and hardware experiments were conducted on the underactuated 18-joint continuum robot "SpiRobs" and a 3-joint robotic finger, showing that MuJoCable faithfully reproduces the phenomenon where joint rotation is redistributed proximally due to guide friction.

This approach allows engineers to evaluate the impact of physical cable threading and guide friction on overall robot motion in simulation before fabrication, substantially reducing trial-and-error cycles in mechanical design and actuator sizing.
contributions: Proposed an algorithm that optimizes a continuous cable path across adjacent moving analytic and mesh surfaces at each step, naturally determining moment arms and stroke from noncircular rolling contact.

Integrated a unilateral axial elasticity law (pull-only), directional Capstan friction, and rigid-body coupling via nodal virtual work, formulating slack, segment tension decay, and redistribution of joint motion.
Implemented and open-sourced the method as a MuJoCo engine plugin that can be flexibly defined via MJCF and operates fast at 11.9x real time thanks to warm-starting.

sections.heading: Why We Need a Renewed Cable Transmission Model
sections.summary: In tendon-driven robots, cable routing, contact surfaces, and friction govern motion and force transfer, yet existing rigid-body simulators cannot resolve them simultaneously. MuJoCable embeds a reduced-order surface routing and friction propagation model as a MuJoCo plugin, aiming to close the sim-to-real gap of transmissions during the design stage.
sections.details:
In robotic hands, continuum robots, and rolling contact joints, cable actuation is indispensable for placing actuators at the base to reduce distal weight and gain compliance. However, when a motor retracts a cable, the robot moves, and as the robot moves, the cable's path, contact points, and moment arms change constantly. Furthermore, friction at eyelets (guide holes) and wrapping surfaces causes tension to become non-uniform across segments. Especially in underactuated robots, this coupling spans multiple joints, so identical cable retraction can produce completely different postures and torques.

Native MuJoCo tendons (spatial tendons) compute the shortest path connecting fixed sites and spherical or cylindrical wrapping geometries. However, multiple obstacles require partition sites, and smooth contact movement over noncircular surfaces cannot be handled. In addition, tension follows Hooke's law around a rest length, meaning cables exert a "pushing force" when compressed. On the other hand, beam models (such as Cosserat rods) that solve cables in free space can capture mass, bending, and torsion, but they are over-engineered for taut in-robot transmissions because they introduce far too many state variables.

MuJoCable treats the cable as a massless, quasi-static elastic line. It combines geometric optimization over moving surfaces, a unilateral tension model, and friction propagation using the Capstan equation. This allows simulation of motion changes caused by actual physical threading while keeping computational costs low.

In bio-inspired rolling joints, contact migration over surfaces and friction dominate; native MuJoCo tendons fail to represent them, whereas MuJoCable correctly resolves continuous surface paths and friction.

sections.heading: Where Existing Cable Representations and Friction Models Stand
sections.summary: Cable models in robotics simulation span simple shortest geometric paths to high-fidelity beam models, but reduced-order methods resolving both moving contact and segment friction have been lacking. Friction models also needed a mechanism to feed tension changes directly back into rigid-body dynamics coupled with path geometry.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Cable Representations in Robot Simulation
Musculoskeletal tools like OpenSim compute geometric paths using simple wrap geometries, but they cannot handle directional friction losses from robot guide holes. Musculoskeletal models on MuJoCo (such as MyoSim and EquiMus) support contact-rich environments, yet they lack contact line models that move across noncircular surfaces. Meanwhile, slender beam models are well-suited for solving slack, buckling, and knotting, but they add excessive state variables for taut, short robot transmissions.

### 2.2 Friction Transmission Models
For friction in sheath tubes and guide eyelets, analytical models, complementarity problem approaches, and learning-based methods exist that account for elasticity, backlash, and hysteresis. However, these assume a predefined path geometry and cannot be applied directly to mechanisms where wrapping angles change dynamically with robot motion. This study focuses on the sustained sliding regime common in robot transmissions and adopts an approach that directly computes tension propagation from wrapping angles using the Capstan friction equation.

sections.heading: Core Technology Unifying Surface Optimization, Unilateral Tension, and Friction Propagation
sections.summary: The shortest path is optimized at each time step based on endpoints, guide holes, and guide surfaces defined in MJCF. Unilateral tension is computed from the resulting path length, propagated to each segment's tension via the Capstan equation, and converted into action forces on rigid links via the principle of virtual work.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Scope and Assumptions
The scope covers taut transmission systems, neglecting cable mass, bending stiffness, and wave phenomena. The method assumes quasi-static path finding and sustained sliding friction, delegating rigid-body collisions and time integration to the core MuJoCo engine.

### 3.2 Cable Representation and Problem Formulation
Cables are defined using `user`-attributed sites in MJCF. Here, $user=1$ designates an endpoint, $user=3$ is a physical passing guide hole (hard guide), and $user=2$ provides an initial topological hint specifying surface sequence and wrapping side. At each step $k$ during simulation, the optimal path $\bm{q}_k$ is used to obtain the optimal path $\gamma_k^*$ and path length $L_k$, and generalized forces $\bm{Q}_{c,k}$ corresponding to actuator shortening $c_k$ are applied to the rigid-body system.

### 3.3 Core Transmission Model Components
- **Surface Routing and Geometric Kinematics**: Analytical common tangents are used for cylindrical surfaces, while on mesh surfaces, crossing points on a specified triangular corridor are optimized under non-penetration constraints. Solving entry and exit points between adjacent surfaces simultaneously prevents unnatural kinks at boundaries.
- **Unilateral Tension Response (Unilateral Law)**: Effective elongation $e$ is calculated from the difference between cable length $L$ and free length $L_f$. Introducing a $C^1$-smooth onset function $\psi_a$ ensures tension and damping become strictly zero when $e \leq 0$, realizing a true "slack" state without any pushing forces like Hookean springs.
- **Direction-Dependent Segment Friction (Capstan Propagation)**: At each contact point $i$, tension is propagated sequentially using wrapping angle $\phi_i$, friction coefficient $\mu_i$, and sliding direction $\sigma_i$ via $T_{i} = T_{i-1} \exp(-\sigma_i \mu_i \phi_i)$. This reproduces the phenomenon where tension decays (or builds up) from proximal to distal ends.
- **Coupling to Rigid Bodies**: Internal forces $\bm{f}_i$ acting on contact points are computed from tension vector differences at each node and applied to bodies via MuJoCo's `mj_applyFT`. When computing generalized forces $\bm{Q}_c$ through Jacobians $\bm{J}_i$, virtual work guarantees that the result matches MuJoCo's scalar length gradient when friction is zero.

sections.heading: Three-Tiered Rigorous Validation: From Theoretical Pulleys to Multi-Joint Physical Robots
sections.summary: The method was evaluated across three tiers: comparison with analytical solutions using pulley systems, behavioral differences against native MuJoCo tendons on an 18-joint robot, and sim-to-real reproducibility tests on 3D-printed hardware. It accurately reproduced friction-induced joint rotation bias and tension growth while running at over 10x real time.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted at three hierarchical levels: comparisons with theoretical values (seven pulley systems), cross-simulation comparisons (a rolling joint and the 18-joint logarithmic spiral robot SpiRobs), and hardware validation (SpiRobs and a 3-joint underactuated finger).

### 4.2 Pulley Benchmarks (Agreement with Theory)
Across seven pulley configurations—including fixed pulleys, movable pulleys, and Atwood machines—cable displacement, torque, and Capstan transmission ratios were compared against analytical solutions. The Capstan ratio error was under 0.5%, and the maximum tangent residual was $7.2 \times 10^{-8}$, showing extremely high accuracy. In a free pulley with friction coefficient $\mu=0.15$, the rotational torque arising from the tension difference across sides functioned correctly, perfectly reproducing the onset of pulley rotation at $0.605$ rad/s.

### 4.3 Simulation Comparisons
- **Rolling Joint**: In a finger PIP joint model, constraining with a virtual hinge yielded $49.994^\circ$ of rotation, whereas MuJoCable yielded $52.481^\circ$ by resolving moving contact sliding over surfaces, naturally revealing a geometric discrepancy of $2.487^\circ$.
- **SpiRobs (Comparison with Native Tendons)**: On the 18-joint robot, native tendons and MuJoCable exhibited nearly identical bent shapes outwardly. However, the maximum cable tension resolved by MuJoCable was approximately 4 times higher, and the required cable retraction was about 9% larger. This highlights that internal transmission loads can differ drastically even when external deformations look alike.
- **Guide Friction Sweep**: Sweeping the friction coefficient $\mu$ from 0 to 0.60 caused proximal actuation tension to jump more than fourfold, strongly suppressing distal joint rotation and biasing motion toward proximal joints (Fig. F6 (b)).
- **Computation Speed**: For the 18-joint model, MuJoCable's median step time was 41.96 $\mu$s compared to 34.25 $\mu$s for native tendons (a +22.5% overhead), maintaining a high speed of 11.9x real time with a 0.5 ms step size.

### 4.4 Hardware Validation
When identical retraction sequences were applied to physical SpiRobs hardware and a tendon-driven finger prototype, the bending posture progressions between simulation and hardware matched remarkably well.

sections.heading: Significance as a Design Tool and Current Limitations
sections.summary: Rather than relying solely on control parameter tuning, this approach provides powerful guidelines to inspect cable routing and reduce guide friction (e.g., adding lubrication) before fabrication. Although the routing topology (wrapping sequence) currently needs to be known beforehand, it significantly accelerates hardware iteration.
sections.details:
In underactuated robots, cable transmissions are not merely power delivery systems; they are "the mechanism itself." By using MuJoCable, phenomena often dismissed as sim-to-real discrepancies (such as torque loss and slack caused by guide friction) can be isolated and evaluated geometrically and mechanically.

During the authors' development of the 3-joint finger prototype, the simulator's diagnostic features traced the cause of a malfunction in the initial model to an abrupt tension drop at a specific guide hole. They resolved the issue through localized lubrication and routing revisions. This is a prime example of feeding insights back into mechanical improvements rather than forcing an adjustment via controller gains.

A current limitation is that dynamic topological transitions—such as cables completely derailing from guides—are not supported. Future extensions will be needed to simulate re-engagement or extreme operational envelopes where derailment could occur.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Establishing a Simulation Foundation for Physical Routing
sections.summary: MuJoCable is the first general-purpose rigid-body simulator plugin capable of faithfully reproducing physical cable threading. Its validity and speed have been demonstrated from analytical benchmarks to hardware experiments, establishing it as a promising foundation for future tendon-driven robot design and reinforcement learning control.
sections.details:
MuJoCable combines path optimization over moving multiple surfaces, a unilateral tension law, and Capstan friction propagation to make physical cable threading executable within MuJoCo. Its high-precision mechanical fidelity (under 0.5% error on pulley benchmarks), agreement with physical SpiRobs and underactuated fingers, and fast computation at 11.9x real time have been confirmed.

Thanks to this work, engineers can optimize cable material selection, pretension, actuator sizing, and routing paths on a physics-based foundation before cutting metal. Future work is expected to focus on automated routing topology optimization and applying the framework to high-precision reinforcement learning policy training for tendon-driven robots.

takeaways: In tendon-driven robots, guide friction and contact migration fundamentally alter motion distribution across joints even with the same cable retraction, making transmission modeling indispensable.
MuJoCo native tendons' drawbacks—generating pushing forces and ignoring friction losses—can be resolved while preserving high computational speed using a reduced-order optimization plugin.
Visualizing and diagnosing segment tensions and slack in simulation enables identifying actuator requirements and lubrication needs prior to physical prototyping.
limitations: Dynamic changes in routing topology—such as cables derailing from guides or pulleys, or catching onto new obstacles—are not supported.
Micro-stiction, stick-slip, and pre-sliding hysteresis inside sheath conduits are not captured due to the sustained sliding model formulation.
Dynamic free-cable behaviors resulting from mass and bending stiffness, such as large slack waves in free space, fall outside the model's scope.
